subfields.name: Quantum computing & algorithms
subfields.plain: Using qubits to solve problems faster than normal computers can: searching, factoring, optimisation and simulation.
subfields.phd: Designing new algorithms, proving speed-ups, or working out what near-term machines can really do. Mix of maths, computer science and physics.

subfields.name: Error correction & fault tolerance
subfields.plain: Qubits are fragile. Error correction spreads one 'logical' qubit over many physical ones so mistakes can be caught and fixed.
subfields.phd: Inventing codes and decoders, simulating them, and working with hardware teams. Very hot field with lots of jobs.

subfields.name: Quantum information & entanglement
subfields.plain: The theory of what information looks like when it is quantum: entanglement, measurement, channels and resources.
subfields.phd: Mostly pen-and-paper theory and some numerics. Good if you love clean mathematical ideas.

subfields.name: Quantum communication & cryptography
subfields.plain: Sending quantum states between places: unhackable keys, quantum networks and the future quantum internet.
subfields.phd: Protocol design and security proofs, or building fibre and satellite links in the lab.

subfields.name: Sensing & metrology
subfields.plain: Using quantum effects to measure time, fields, gravity and tiny forces more precisely than ever.
subfields.phd: Often lab-based: atomic clocks, NV-diamond sensors, interferometers. Very practical with real-world uses.

subfields.name: Quantum optics & photonics
subfields.plain: Light at the level of single photons: lasers, cavities, squeezed light and photonic chips.
subfields.phd: Hands-on optics labs or theory of light–matter interaction. Many skills transfer to industry.

subfields.name: Atoms, ions & cold gases
subfields.plain: Trapping and cooling atoms and ions to nearly absolute zero so their quantum nature shows up clearly.
subfields.phd: Big table-top experiments with lasers and vacuum, or theory that models them. Great for quantum simulation too.

subfields.name: Condensed matter & quantum materials
subfields.plain: How huge numbers of electrons and spins behave together: superconductors, magnets, topological phases.
subfields.phd: Huge field: theory, computation or experiments on new materials. Lots of open mysteries.

subfields.name: Qubit hardware & devices
subfields.plain: Building the actual qubits: superconducting circuits, spins in silicon, trapped ions, neutral atoms and photons.
subfields.phd: Engineering-flavoured physics: fabrication, microwave control, cryogenics, calibration.

subfields.name: Open systems & thermodynamics
subfields.plain: What happens when quantum systems leak into their surroundings: noise, decoherence, heat and quantum engines.
subfields.phd: Theory with a lot of differential equations and numerics, linked to almost every experiment.

subfields.name: Foundations of quantum mechanics
subfields.plain: The big questions: what measurement really means, Bell tests, contextuality and interpretations.
subfields.phd: Conceptual and mathematical. Small field, deep questions, sometimes paired with experiments.

subfields.name: Fields, gravity & cosmology
subfields.plain: Quantum physics at the largest and smallest scales: black holes, holography, quantum fields and the early universe.
subfields.phd: Heavy maths: field theory, string theory, quantum gravity. Increasingly connected to quantum information.

subfields.name: Quantum simulation & chemistry
subfields.plain: Using quantum machines or clever classical methods to simulate molecules, materials and many-body dynamics.
subfields.phd: Computational and algorithmic. Useful for chemistry, materials and drug design.

subfields.name: Quantum machine learning
subfields.plain: Mixing quantum computing with machine learning, and using AI to help run quantum experiments.
subfields.phd: Young, fast-moving field between computer science and physics. Good if you like coding.

concepts.name: Qubit
concepts.plain: The quantum version of a bit. It can be 0, 1, or a blend of both at once until you look.

concepts.name: Superposition
concepts.plain: A quantum thing can be in several states at once, like a coin spinning in the air rather than heads or tails.

concepts.name: Interference
concepts.plain: When quantum possibilities add up or cancel out, like ripples on a pond meeting each other.

concepts.name: Wave–particle duality
concepts.plain: Particles like electrons travel like waves but land like dots. The double-slit experiment shows both at once.

concepts.name: Entanglement
concepts.plain: Two particles share one joint state, so measuring one instantly tells you about the other, however far apart.

concepts.name: Bell tests & nonlocality
concepts.plain: Experiments that prove nature can't be explained by hidden instructions carried inside particles.

concepts.name: Measurement
concepts.plain: Looking at a quantum system forces it to pick an answer, and changes it in the process.

concepts.name: Interpretations & contextuality
concepts.plain: Different stories about what quantum mechanics really says about reality. The maths is the same; the meaning is debated.

concepts.name: Tunnelling
concepts.plain: A quantum particle can pass through a wall it doesn't have the energy to climb over.

concepts.name: Harmonic oscillator & phonons
concepts.plain: A quantum spring. Its energy comes in equal steps, and this simple model describes light, sound and vibrations.

concepts.name: Decoherence & noise
concepts.plain: The surroundings slowly 'peek' at a quantum system and wash out its quantum behaviour. The enemy of quantum computers.

concepts.name: Open quantum systems
concepts.plain: Quantum systems that exchange energy or information with their environment, which is all real ones.

concepts.name: Quantum thermodynamics
concepts.plain: Heat, work and engines when the parts are quantum. Can quantum effects make better batteries or fridges?

concepts.name: Driving & Rabi oscillations
concepts.plain: Shining the right frequency of light or microwaves on an atom or qubit makes it flip back and forth between states.

concepts.name: Superconducting qubits
concepts.plain: Tiny electrical circuits cooled near absolute zero that behave like artificial atoms. Used by Google and IBM.

concepts.name: Spin qubits & defects
concepts.plain: Qubits made from the spin of a single electron or nucleus, held in silicon chips or diamond defects.

concepts.name: Trapped ions
concepts.plain: Single charged atoms held in place by electric fields and controlled with lasers. Very clean qubits.

concepts.name: Neutral atoms & Rydberg
concepts.plain: Arrays of single atoms held by laser 'tweezers'. Excite them to giant Rydberg states and they interact strongly.

concepts.name: Cold atoms & condensates
concepts.plain: Gases cooled to billionths of a degree, where millions of atoms can act like one giant quantum wave.

concepts.name: Atomic clocks & spectroscopy
concepts.plain: Clocks that tick with atoms. The best ones would lose less than a second over the age of the universe.

concepts.name: Quantum sensing
concepts.plain: Using superposition and entanglement as an ultra-sensitive ruler for fields, time and motion.

concepts.name: Single photons & photonics
concepts.plain: Particles of light. They are fast, don't easily get noisy, and are great for carrying quantum information.

concepts.name: Light–matter interaction
concepts.plain: When light and matter trade energy back and forth so fast they form a new hybrid thing.

concepts.name: Quantum key distribution
concepts.plain: Making secret keys with photons. Any spy who looks leaves fingerprints, so you know if the key is safe.

concepts.name: Quantum networks & repeaters
concepts.plain: Linking quantum devices over distance so they can share entanglement, the backbone of a future quantum internet.

concepts.name: Quantum algorithms
concepts.plain: Step-by-step recipes for quantum computers. A few of them are provably much faster than any classical recipe.

concepts.name: Variational & near-term algorithms
concepts.plain: Hybrid tricks where a normal computer tunes the knobs of a small, noisy quantum circuit to find good answers.

concepts.name: Quantum advantage & complexity
concepts.plain: Proving (or disproving) that a quantum computer can do a task no classical computer could do in reasonable time.

concepts.name: Quantum circuits & gates
concepts.plain: Quantum programs are written as circuits: a sequence of gates that rotate and connect qubits.

concepts.name: Error-correcting codes
concepts.plain: Storing one reliable qubit in many unreliable ones, then checking for and fixing errors without destroying the data.

concepts.name: Fault tolerance & thresholds
concepts.plain: If each part fails rarely enough (below a 'threshold'), you can make computations as reliable as you like.

concepts.name: Spin chains & magnetism
concepts.plain: Rows of tiny magnets (spins) that talk to their neighbours. Simple to write down, but full of surprising behaviour.

concepts.name: Many-body dynamics
concepts.plain: How information and energy spread through a big quantum system after you poke it.

concepts.name: Disorder & localisation
concepts.plain: Enough randomness can trap quantum waves in place, so they stop spreading. This is called localisation.

concepts.name: Topological phases
concepts.plain: Phases of matter whose properties are protected by shape-like (topological) rules, making them very robust.

concepts.name: Superconductivity
concepts.plain: Some materials carry electricity with exactly zero resistance when cold. Explaining the 'high temperature' ones is still open.

concepts.name: 2D & quantum materials
concepts.plain: Materials only one atom thick, or with unusual crystal patterns, where electrons act in strange new ways.

concepts.name: Quantum phase transitions
concepts.plain: Like ice melting, but at absolute zero and driven by quantum fluctuations instead of heat.

concepts.name: Tensor networks & numerics
concepts.plain: Clever ways for ordinary computers to handle quantum systems that look far too big to fit in memory.

concepts.name: Quantum simulation
concepts.plain: Using one controllable quantum system to mimic another that is too hard to study directly.

concepts.name: Quantum chemistry
concepts.plain: Working out how electrons arrange themselves in molecules, which decides how chemicals react.

concepts.name: Quantum walks & transport
concepts.plain: A quantum 'drunkard's walk' that spreads much faster than a normal random walk, thanks to interference.

concepts.name: Machine learning
concepts.plain: Teaching computers from data. Here, either running learning on quantum computers or using AI to do physics.

concepts.name: Entanglement entropy
concepts.plain: A number that measures how much one part of a system is entangled with the rest.

concepts.name: Channels & resource theories
concepts.plain: The rules for how quantum information can be moved, measured and turned into useful 'fuel'.

concepts.name: Randomness & benchmarking
concepts.plain: Using randomness to test how good a quantum device is, or to certify that numbers are truly random.

concepts.name: Black holes & information
concepts.plain: Do black holes destroy information? Quantum physics says no, and working out how is a famous puzzle.

concepts.name: Holography & AdS/CFT
concepts.plain: The idea that a universe with gravity can be fully described by a quantum system on its boundary, like a hologram.

concepts.name: Quantum field theory
concepts.plain: The language of particle physics: every particle is a ripple in a field that fills all of space.

concepts.name: Quantum gravity & cosmology
concepts.plain: Joining quantum physics with Einstein's gravity, from the Big Bang to whether gravity itself is quantum.

concepts.name: Uncertainty & quantum limits
concepts.plain: Some pairs of things, like position and speed, can't both be pinned down exactly. Nature has built-in fuzziness.
